techniques.name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
techniques.description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

A recruitment agency requires a named recruiter to confirm or reverse every automated rejection before it is sent, and logs the decision and the reason. The agency's governance board reviews the override rate each quarter to see whether the screening tool and its reviewers are working as intended.

limitations.description: Review capacity sets a ceiling. As volume rises, cases queue, decisions are delayed and time-sensitive uses become impractical, so the escalation rules must be tuned to what the available trained reviewers can handle.
Reviewers tire and drift. Attention and consistency fall over a long shift or a run of similar cases, so two reviewers, or one reviewer at different times, may decide the same case differently.

Automation bias. People tend to accept a system's recommendation, particularly under time pressure, so review can become a rubber stamp. A very high approval rate with almost no overrides may signal this rather than a good system.

The escalation rules decide what a human ever sees. A confidently wrong output passes without review when only low-confidence cases are escalated, so reviewing a random sample of routine cases is needed to find these errors.

Human review does not reliably improve decisions. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found human-AI combinations performed worse on average than the better of human or AI alone, with losses in decision-making tasks. The effect of a checkpoint should be tested, not assumed.

resources.title: Improving the Applicability of AI for Psychiatric Applications through Human-in-the-loop Methodologies
resources.abstract: Objectives Machine learning (ML) and natural language processing have great potential to improve efficiency and accuracy in diagnosis, treatment recommendations, predictive interventions, and scarce resource allocation within psychiatry. Researchers often conceptualize such an approach as operating in isolation without much need for human involvement, yet it remains crucial to harness human-in-the-loop practices when developing and implementing such techniques as their absence may be catastrophic. We advocate for building ML-based technologies that collaborate with experts within psychiatry in all stages of implementation and use to increase model performance while simultaneously increasing the practicality, robustness, and reliability of the process. Methods We showcase pitfalls of the traditional ML framework and explain how it can be improved with human-in-the-loop techniques. Specifically, we applied active learning strategies to the automatic scoring of a story recall task and compared the results to a traditional approach. Results Human-in-the-loop methodologies supplied a greater understanding of where the model was least confident or had knowledge gaps during training. As compared to the traditional framework, less than half of the training data were needed to reach a given accuracy. Conclusions Human-in-the-loop ML is an approach to data collection and model creation that harnesses active learning to select the most critical data needed to increase a model’s accuracy and generalizability more efficiently than classic random sampling would otherwise allow. Such techniques may additionally operate as safeguards from spurious predictions and can aid in decreasing disparities that artificial intelligence systems otherwise propagate.

resources.title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
resources.abstract: Technical developments in computer hardware and software now make it possible to introduce automation into virtually all aspects of human-machine systems. Given these technical capabilities, which system functions should be automated and to what extent? We outline a model for types and levels of automation that provides a framework and an objective basis for making such choices. Appropriate selection is important because automation does not merely supplant but changes human activity and can impose new coordination demands on the human operator. We propose that automation can be applied to four broad classes of functions: 1) information acquisition; 2) information analysis; 3) decision and action selection; and 4) action implementation. Within each of these types, automation can be applied across a continuum of levels from low to high, i.e., from fully manual to fully automatic. A particular system can involve automation of all four types at different levels. The human performance consequences of particular types and levels of automation constitute primary evaluative criteria for automation design using our model. Secondary evaluative criteria include automation reliability and the costs of decision/action consequences, among others. Examples of recommended types and levels of automation are provided to illustrate the application of the model to automation design.

resources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resources.abstract: Inspired by the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) to augment humans, researchers have studied human–AI systems involving different tasks, systems and populations. Despite such a large body of work, we lack a broad conceptual understanding of when combinations of humans and AI are better than either alone. Here we addressed this question by conducting a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of 106 experimental studies reporting 370 effect sizes. We searched an interdisciplinary set of databases (the Association for Computing Machinery Digital Library, the Web of Science and the Association for Information Systems eLibrary) for studies published between 1 January 2020 and 30 June 2023. Each study was required to include an original human-participants experiment that evaluated the performance of humans alone, AI alone and human–AI combinations. First, we found that, on average, human–AI combinations performed significantly worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges’ g = −0.23; 95% confidence interval, −0.39 to −0.07). Second, we found performance losses in tasks that involved making decisions and significantly greater gains in tasks that involved creating content. Finally, when humans outperformed AI alone, we found performance gains in the combination, but when AI outperformed humans alone, we found losses. Limitations of the evidence assessed here include possible publication bias and variations in the study designs analysed. Overall, these findings highlight the heterogeneity of the effects of human–AI collaboration and point to promising avenues for improving human–AI systems.

resources.title: Article 14: Human Oversight | EU Artificial Intelligence Act
Human-in-the-loop machine learning: a state of the art
resources.abstract: Researchers are defining new types of interactions between humans and machine learning algorithms generically called human-in-the-loop machine learning. Depending on who is in control of the learning process, we can identify: active learning, in which the system remains in control; interactive machine learning, in which there is a closer interaction between users and learning systems; and machine teaching, where human domain experts have control over the learning process. Aside from control, humans can also be involved in the learning process in other ways. In curriculum learning human domain experts try to impose some structure on the examples presented to improve the learning; in explainable AI the focus is on the ability of the model to explain to humans why a given solution was chosen. This collaboration between AI models and humans should not be limited only to the learning process; if we go further, we can see other terms that arise such as Usable and Useful AI. In this paper we review the state of the art of the techniques involved in the new forms of relationship between humans and ML algorithms. Our contribution is not merely listing the different approaches, but to provide definitions clarifying confusing, varied and sometimes contradictory terms; to elucidate and determine the boundaries between the different methods; and to correlate all the techniques searching for the connections and influences between them.

techniques.name: Confidence Thresholding
techniques.description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing tiered confidence thresholds in autonomous vehicle decision-making where high-confidence lane changes (>98%) execute automatically, medium-confidence decisions (85-98%) trigger additional sensor verification, and low-confidence situations (<85%) engage conservative defensive driving modes or request human takeover.

A diabetic eye-screening service has its image classifier pass the cases it is least sure about to an ophthalmologist. The service picks the referral share, for example the least certain 10 to 20 per cent of images, so that accuracy on the cases handled automatically meets its target.

A payment processor's fraud model approves transactions it scores as clearly legitimate, runs extra automated checks on middling scores, and sends the least certain ones to an analyst. The thresholds are set so that the analyst queue stays within the team's daily capacity.

A council's tool that flags possible errors in benefit claims shows caseworkers whether each flag is above or below its confidence threshold. The council publishes the share of claims sent to manual review and the error rate among those handled automatically, so the public can see when the tool declines to decide.

limitations.description: Many models produce poorly calibrated confidence scores that don't accurately reflect true prediction uncertainty, leading to overconfident predictions for incorrect outputs or underconfident scores for correct predictions.

Threshold selection requires careful calibration and domain expertise, as inappropriate thresholds can either overwhelm human reviewers with too many cases or miss genuinely uncertain decisions that need oversight.

High-confidence predictions may still be incorrect or harmful, particularly when models encounter adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution data, or systematic biases that the confidence mechanism doesn't detect.
Static thresholds may become inappropriate over time as model performance degrades, data distribution shifts occur, or operational contexts change, requiring ongoing monitoring and adjustment.
Withholding a prediction does not make the subsequent process safe. Review delays, failed routing and inadequate fallback capacity can undermine the intended safeguard.

resources.abstract: The performance of a pattern recognition system is characterized by its error and reject tradeoff. resources.title: Improving speech recognition accuracy with multi-confidence thresholding
Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

sample_claims.text: The vehicle's planner switches to its conservative fallback whenever perception confidence falls below the validated threshold.
Screening results the model is least certain about are referred to a clinician, and the error rate among results released without review stays within the clinical target at the chosen threshold.
Transactions scoring below the review threshold go to an analyst, and the resulting review queue stays within the fraud team's agreed daily capacity.
The deferral rate and the error rate among automatically handled cases at the operating threshold are documented and reported to the oversight board.
Each prediction shown to staff carries its confidence level, and predictions below the threshold are labelled as low confidence.

techniques.name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
techniques.description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

example_use_cases.description: A fraud-scoring API provider examines each client's query stream for runs of near-identical transactions altered in small steps, which suggest someone is probing for the score at which a transaction passes. Flagged accounts are rate-limited and sent to the security team for review.

A company selling traffic-sign recognition as a paid API tests whether the spacing between each customer's successive image queries follows the pattern ordinary use produces. Accounts whose queries look synthetic and widely spread, as in model-copying attacks, are flagged for investigation and possible suspension.

A health-technology company serving a paediatric triage model to many clinics monitors each clinic's query volumes and the ages in its requests. A clinic sending mostly adult patients, or a sudden change after a software update, is flagged so the company can contact it before unsafe advice is given.

A provider of a text-generation API scores each customer's usage by how often prompts and responses are flagged as harmful and whether jailbreak attempts recur. Customers with high scores go to review, which can lead to a warning or suspension.

A bank's model risk team compares the monthly log of calls to its credit-scoring API, by internal team and purpose, with the uses approved at validation. The comparison is filed in the model's audit record, so reviewers can see whether the model is used as documented.

limitations.description: Anomalies are defined against a baseline of normal use, and ordinary users can be unusual. In PRADA's tests, legitimate queries made of consecutive frames from a sequence triggered false alarms at stricter settings, so the alert threshold has to be tuned to each model and use case.

A patient attacker can stay inside normal limits by querying slowly, adding dummy queries or spreading queries across many accounts. PRADA's authors show that padding queries raises the attacker's cost three to ten times, and that multiple accounts defeat per-account analysis.

Useful monitoring needs request content, or features of it, to be logged and sometimes read by reviewers. For sensitive applications that may be unlawful or unacceptable, and Microsoft notes that detection may be less accurate when human review is switched off for such customers.

Detectors keep state for every account. PRADA's authors estimate a few gigabytes in total for a few hundred clients of an image model, and the cost rises with traffic and with the retention period set for audit evidence.

The published extraction detectors were tested on small models, decision trees in one case and image classifiers in the other, against simulated attackers. Kesarwani et al. describe their warning as approximate, so an alert is a lead for investigation, not proof of theft.

resources.title: Model Extraction Warning in MLaaS Paradigm
resources.abstract: Machine learning models deployed on the cloud are susceptible to several security threats including extraction attacks. Adversaries may abuse a model's prediction API to steal the model thus compromising model confidentiality, privacy of training data, and revenue from future query payments. This work introduces a model extraction monitor that quantifies the extraction status of models by continually observing the API query and response streams of users. We present two novel strategies that measure either the information gain or the coverage of the feature space spanned by user queries to estimate the learning rate of individual and colluding adversaries. Both approaches have low computational overhead and can easily be offered as services to model owners to warn them against state of the art extraction attacks. We demonstrate empirical performance results of these approaches for decision tree and neural network models using open source datasets and BigML MLaaS platform.

resources.title: PRADA: Protecting Against DNN Model Stealing Attacks
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) applications are increasingly prevalent. Protecting the confidentiality of ML models becomes paramount for two reasons: (a) a model can be a business advantage to its owner, and (b) an adversary may use a stolen model to find transferable adversarial examples that can evade classification by the original model. Access to the model can be restricted to be only via well-defined prediction APIs. Nevertheless, prediction APIs still provide enough information to allow an adversary to mount model extraction attacks by sending repeated queries via the prediction API. In this paper, we describe new model extraction attacks using novel approaches for generating synthetic queries, and optimizing training hyperparameters. Our attacks outperform state-of-the-art model extraction in terms of transferability of both targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples (up to +29-44 percentage points, pp), and prediction accuracy (up to +46 pp) on two datasets. We provide take-aways on how to perform effective model extraction attacks. We then propose PRADA, the first step towards generic and effective detection of DNN model extraction attacks. It analyzes the distribution of consecutive API queries and raises an alarm when this distribution deviates from benign behavior. We show that PRADA can detect all prior model extraction attacks with no false positives.

techniques.name: Out-of-Domain Detection
techniques.description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Scope is defined by examples, such as an assistant's supported intents (the actions it can recognise), and a detector then scores how closely each new query resembles them. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. A query judged out of scope can be declined, handed to a person or another service, or answered with a request to rephrase, instead of receiving an unreliable or invented answer. The detector tests resemblance to the defined scope, not what the system actually knows, so it needs evaluating on realistic out-of-scope queries.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a medical chatbot specialised in diabetes management to recognise and deflect questions about unrelated conditions, avoiding potentially dangerous medical advice outside its training domain.

Ensuring an educational AI tutor for high school mathematics reliably identifies advanced university-level questions and redirects students to appropriate resources rather than attempting explanations beyond its scope.

An insurer's claims-intake assistant is built for routine motor and household claims. Messages about unfamiliar claim types, such as large flood events or commercial losses, are detected and routed to a specialist adjuster instead of being handled with irrelevant questions.

A council's resident-services chatbot covers bin collections, parking permits and council tax. When a resident asks about something it does not cover, such as a planning dispute, it says so, names the service that can help and logs the query, and the log shows the council which topics residents ask about that the chatbot cannot answer.

limitations.description: Scope has to be defined before it can be detected, and general-purpose assistants or fuzzy domains have no clean edge. A narrow definition refuses legitimate queries, and a loose one lets unsupported queries through.

Detection is weakest on queries that resemble in-scope ones. In the 2019 benchmark that introduced the task, no intent classifier caught more than about two-thirds of out-of-scope queries even when trained on examples of them, so recall should be measured on realistic out-of-scope queries before the detector is relied on.
The threshold trades wrongly refusing valid queries against wrongly answering unsupported ones. The two errors rarely cost the same, and queries near the boundary will still land on both sides.
Users can rephrase or disguise an unsupported request so that it resembles in-scope wording. A detector tested only on plain phrasings overstates how well it holds up against paraphrase.

Scope changes as capabilities are added or retired, so the detector and its out-of-scope test set need refreshing, or it will refuse newly supported queries and accept newly unsupported ones. Building realistic out-of-scope examples is costly because annotators need expert knowledge of the in-scope intents.

resources.title: An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction
resources.abstract: Task-oriented dialog systems need to know when a query falls outside their range of supported intents, but current text classification corpora only define label sets that cover every example. We introduce a new dataset that includes queries that are out-of-scope—i.e., queries that do not fall into any of the system’s supported intents. This poses a new challenge because models cannot assume that every query at inference time belongs to a system-supported intent class. Our dataset also covers 150 intent classes over 10 domains, capturing the breadth that a production task-oriented agent must handle. We evaluate a range of benchmark classifiers on our dataset along with several different out-of-scope identification schemes. We find that while the classifiers perform well on in-scope intent classification, they struggle to identify out-of-scope queries. Our dataset and evaluation fill an important gap in the field, offering a way of more rigorously and realistically benchmarking text classification in task-driven dialog systems.

techniques.name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
techniques.description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.

techniques.name: Explanation Satisfaction Scale
techniques.description: The Explanation Satisfaction Scale is a short questionnaire on which people who have used an AI system's explanations rate how satisfying and sufficient they found them; Hoffman, Mueller, Klein and Litman developed it in the DARPA Explainable AI programme to capture the user's judgement of an explanation, as distinct from a researcher's judgement of its quality. Each item is a statement about the explanation, for example that from it the user understands how the system works, or that it is satisfying, has sufficient detail, seems complete, tells the user how to use the system, is useful to their goals or shows how accurate the system is, and each is rated on a five-point scale from 'I agree strongly' to 'I disagree strongly'. Participants complete it after they have worked with the system and received explanations, usually once for each explanation condition in a study that compares conditions; the published form sets no scoring rule or threshold, and the implementation by one of its authors in the OpenScales library scores it as the mean of the item ratings. Versions differ: the authors' 2018 report gives eight items, their 2023 journal article seven (it drops the item on knowing when to trust the system), and the form on the XAITK site nine (it adds an item on reliability), with a note that researchers may use a subset. The score measures how users judge an explanation, not whether they understood it or decide better with it, and the authors present it beside separate measures of mental models, trust and task performance.

example_use_cases.description: A research team comparing counterfactual images with saliency heatmaps (LIME and layer-wise relevance propagation) for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier gives lay participants the scale after they have predicted the classifier's decision on a set of images. It chooses which explanation to develop on prediction accuracy and uses the ratings only as a second check, so that the explanation people prefer is not assumed to be the one they understand better.

A team deciding whether causal explanations of a reinforcement-learning agent's strategy in a real-time strategy game are worth the extra modelling gives participants the scale after each explained gameplay video. It compares the causal explanations with a simpler explanation and with no explanation on four items (understanding, satisfaction, sufficient detail and completeness), and pairs the ratings with a test of whether participants can predict the agent's next action.

A lender piloting a new letter that explains which factors led to a credit refusal asks pilot applicants to complete the scale after reading either the new letter or the current one. It uses the items on sufficient detail and usefulness to decide whether to add the sentence, held back so far, that says what change would have led to approval.

limitations.description: A high rating does not show that people understand the system or decide better with it. Hase and Bansal found no evidence that participants' ratings of explanation quality predicted whether the explanations helped them predict the model, Buçinca et al. found that subjective measures did not predict performance on the real decision task, and the scale's authors note that people can feel satisfied while their understanding is piecemeal or wrong.

The published evidence for the scale is small: content-validity ratings by 35 attendees of a DARPA programme meeting, an internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) of 0.86, and eight volunteers rating good and bad explanations of everyday technologies, where the difference was large but only marginally significant. The 2018 report's mean for good explanations (42.75) exceeds what eight items scored 1 to 5 can sum to, so the form tested is unclear, and the XAITK page asks for reliability data.

There are no norms or thresholds, so a score means something only against another condition in the same study, such as the current explanation or no explanation. A mean rating reported on its own, such as 4 out of 5, cannot support a claim that an explanation is satisfactory.

Versions with seven, eight and nine items are in circulation, item wording differs between them, and the form invites researchers to use a subset; Madumal et al., for example, report four items. Scores from different studies are therefore not comparable unless the same items and wording were used, and each study should report exactly which it used.

resources.title: Measures for explainable AI: Explanation goodness, user satisfaction, mental models, curiosity, trust, and human-AI performance
Metrics for Explainable AI: Challenges and Prospects
resources.abstract: The question addressed in this paper is: If we present to a user an AI system that explains how it works, how do we know whether the explanation works and the user has achieved a pragmatic understanding of the AI? In other words, how do we know that an explanainable AI system (XAI) is any good? Our focus is on the key concepts of measurement. We discuss specific methods for evaluating: (1) the goodness of explanations, (2) whether users are satisfied by explanations, (3) how well users understand the AI systems, (4) how curiosity motivates the search for explanations, (5) whether the user's trust and reliance on the AI are appropriate, and finally, (6) how the human-XAI work system performs. The recommendations we present derive from our integration of extensive research literatures and our own psychometric evaluations.

techniques.name: Forward Simulation Test
techniques.description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team must choose between feature-attribution bar charts and a short rule list as the explanation shown to credit analysts for a loan-default model. It runs a forward simulation test with 30 credit analysts on past applications, balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions, and adopts the rule list only if its gain over the no-explanation baseline is clearly larger than that of the bar charts; otherwise it treats the two as equal.

An online platform's trust and safety team uses the counterfactual variant to test whether moderators who see which words a toxicity classifier weighted can predict whether it will still flag a comment after one of those words is replaced. A score no better than the baseline tells the team that the highlights do not show how the classifier responds to edits, before it writes moderation guidance that relies on them.

A research team choosing between counterfactual images and saliency heatmaps for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier shows each group of participants explained example images, then asks them to predict the classifier's decision on 12 other images, three from each cell of its confusion matrix, without explanations. It takes forward to a study with clinicians the explanation whose group predicts best, measured against a group that saw the examples without explanations.

A local authority plans to show caseworkers, who are outside the team that built it, the reasons behind a housing-benefit fraud-risk score. Before releasing the reasons in that form, it runs a forward simulation test with caseworkers on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, using the reasons exactly as they will appear, and revises them if caseworkers who studied them predict the flag no better than caseworkers who did not.

limitations.description: A pass shows that people can anticipate the model, not that they decide better with it. Buçinca et al. found that results on a task of predicting an AI's decisions did not predict results on the real decision task, and Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. found that people who could better simulate a simple, clear model did not follow it more when that helped, and in some experiments were less able to correct its large mistakes. A claim about decisions needs a decision study.

The test is easily made trivial. If the explained examples are reused as test items, explanations that show the predicted class or a probability give the answer away, and if the model is mostly right, participants can score well by predicting the true label. Hase and Bansal found earlier studies that reused the same items for explanation and prediction; results from such designs overstate what the explanation conveys.

Effects are often small against the variation between people and items. With 32 trained undergraduates and about 180 to 320 responses per condition, Hase and Bansal's 95% confidence intervals on the change in accuracy were about 8 to 13 percentage points either side, and only LIME on tabular data clearly improved both forward and counterfactual simulation. A study must be sized for the difference it needs to detect, with a bootstrap over both participants and items.

The score holds for the people tested. Many studies use students or crowd workers because domain experts are costly to recruit, which Doshi-Velez and Kim give as the reason this kind of evaluation is cheaper; a result from lay participants does not show that the clinicians, analysts or caseworkers who will use the explanation can predict the model.

The before-and-after design credits any gain to the explanations, but participants see the same examples and test items twice, and Hase and Bansal had no group that repeated both phases without explanations, so a practice gain is not ruled out. Their participants also found it hard to remember the explained examples while predicting, so the number of examples and the time allowed must be fixed and reported when methods are compared.

resources.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.abstract: As machine learning systems become ubiquitous, there has been a surge of interest in interpretable machine learning: systems that provide explanation for their outputs. These explanations are often used to qualitatively assess other criteria such as safety or non-discrimination. However, despite the interest in interpretability, there is very little consensus on what interpretable machine learning is and how it should be measured. In this position paper, we first define interpretability and describe when interpretability is needed (and when it is not). Next, we suggest a taxonomy for rigorous evaluation and expose open questions towards a more rigorous science of interpretable machine learning.

techniques.name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
techniques.description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a nurse-facing explanation for a patient deterioration score runs think-aloud sessions with six ward nurses on a clickable prototype using past patient records. It finds that nurses read a factor that lowered the score as a sign that the patient was improving, relabels the chart, and re-tests the new labels in a second round before fixing the design for a quantitative evaluation.

The developer of a vocal emotion-recognition app that highlights which parts of a recording drove each prediction runs remote think-aloud sessions with a dozen users. One participant reads the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone of voice, a misreading that no rating of the explanation would have revealed, and the team changes how the highlight is drawn.

A bank's model risk team preparing to give loan officers counterfactual explanations (for example, the income at which a refused application would have been approved) runs think-aloud sessions with five officers on past applications, including some the model got wrong. It learns which suggestions officers would pass on to applicants and which they reject as implausible, and decides whether to filter the suggestions before release.

limitations.description: How participants are asked to talk changes what is observed. A meta-analysis of 94 studies by Fox, Ericsson and Best found that plain thinking aloud left accuracy unchanged, but that asking people to explain or describe their thinking changed performance, and that verbal reports of every kind tended to make tasks take longer. Facilitators must avoid 'why' prompts, and task times from these sessions cannot serve as performance measures.

Talking through a task can make people attend to an explanation more than they would at work. In Buçinca et al.'s think-aloud study, participants' preferences between two explanation types matched the results of a proxy task rather than those of the realistic task, and the authors suggest thinking aloud pushed people into analytical thinking, so these sessions may overstate how closely users read explanations in normal use.

Studies use few participants (between 4 and 14 in the sources for this record), so a finding shows that a problem exists, not how common it is, and cannot support a claim about the share of users who understand an explanation or about decision quality. The sessions also show only the situations their tasks include: tasks need some wrong model outputs if the team wants to see how people use an explanation when the model errs.

Not everything people do with an explanation gets said. Quick, perceptual uses leave little trace: in Zhang and Lim's study, participants called the audio examples intuitive but did not say why they found them simple. People also tend to say what they think the right answer is, the social desirability bias the GOV.UK guidance warns of. Silence about part of an explanation does not mean it went unused or was understood, and a screen recording or gaze data is needed to tell these apart.

Findings depend on the analyst: coding transcripts into themes is interpretive, so a study meant to support an assurance claim needs a stated coding scheme and a second coder. The voice and screen recordings are personal data that need participants' consent and controlled storage, and recordings made on real cases may also hold personal data about the people those cases concern.
